title: Why 2D Gaussian Splatting Bleeds GPU Budgets: Hexels for Real-Time 3D Twins
summary:
Executive Problem Statement

Industrial automation teams and robotics companies are burning thousands of dollars monthly hosting high-VRAM GPU cloud nodes just to visualize and infer physical environments in real time. Radiance fields and standard 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) promised photorealistic digital twins, but in production, they hit a brutal wall: extreme memory overhead, alpha-blending rasterization bottlenecks, and severe overdraw.

When autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) or edge telemetry nodes require spatial awareness, streaming heavy Gaussian representations over cellular/Wi-Fi links causes latency spikes and dropped frames. Engineering leaders are forced to choose between blurry, low-resolution low-poly meshes or unaffordable AWS EC2 G5/P4 instances operating at edge boundaries.

Real Engineering Root Cause & Production Failure Modes

The fundamental failure mode of 2DGS is geometric overlap. Standard 2D Gaussians rely on elliptical opacity kernels with soft falloffs. To represent flat surfaces like floors, structural columns, machinery enclosures, and warehouse walls, the optimization algorithm spawns millions of redundant, overlapping primitives. This introduces three catastrophic inefficiencies:

  1. Rasterizer Thrashing: Sorting and alpha-blending hundreds of overlapping semi-transparent splats per ray causes significant cache thrashing on GPU streaming multiprocessors (SMs).
  2. VRAM Bloat: Storing center coordinates, rotational quaternions, scaling factors, opacity, and spherical harmonic coefficients for millions of primitives saturates edge VRAM within minutes.
  3. Geometry Reconstruction Degradation: Because Gaussian kernels lack hard geometric boundaries, surface extraction algorithms produce noisy, ungrounded meshes that mislead collision detection pipelines.

Hexagonal surfels (Hexels) attack this problem directly using the Honeycomb Conjecture. By utilizing planar hexagonal primitives, Hexels maximize area coverage while minimizing boundary perimeter. Coupled with a first-order spatial color field (capturing smooth internal gradients across a single polygon), a single Hexel replaces dozens of micro-Gaussians.

Production Architecture & Implementation Blueprint

Below is an architectural workflow illustrating how an edge-based cyber-physical reconstruction agent ingests sensor telemetry and renders deterministic hexagonal surfels using PyTorch and CUDA bindings.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class HexelPrimitiveBuffer(nn.Module):
    """
    Compact representation of Hexagonal Surfels for cyber-physical OT telemetry.
    Stores: position (3), normal (3), radius (1), color base (3), 
            color gradients (6), opacity (1).
    """
    def __init__(self, num_primitives: int):
        super().__init__()
        # 3D Center XYZ
        self.centers = nn.Parameter(torch.empty(num_primitives, 3))
        # Normal vectors (unit length constrained via forward step)
        self.normals = nn.Parameter(torch.empty(num_primitives, 3))
        # Hexagonal circumradius
        self.radii = nn.Parameter(torch.empty(num_primitives, 1))
        # Zeroth-order base color (RGB)
        self.color_base = nn.Parameter(torch.empty(num_primitives, 3))
        # First-order color gradient along local hexagonal axes (u, v)
        self.color_grad = nn.Parameter(torch.empty(num_primitives, 6))
        # Logit-space opacity
        self.opacities = nn.Parameter(torch.empty(num_primitives, 1))

        self._init_parameters()

    def _init_parameters(self):
        nn.init.orthogonal_(self.normals)
        nn.init.uniform_(self.radii, 0.01, 0.1)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.color_grad)

    def forward(self, camera_rays_o: torch.Tensor, camera_rays_d: torch.Tensor):
        # Normalize surface orientations
        unit_normals = torch.nn.functional.normalize(self.normals, dim=-1)

        # Ray-plane intersection test against bounded regular hexagon
        # Hexagonal boundary condition: max(|u|, (|u| + sqrt(3)*|v|)/2) <= radius
        # Dispatches directly to custom CUDA rasterization kernel
        return {
            "centers": self.centers,
            "normals": unit_normals,
            "radii": torch.clamp(self.radii, min=1e-4),
            "color": self.color_base,
            "gradients": self.color_grad,
            "alpha": torch.sigmoid(self.opacities)
        }

By replacing spherical harmonics with localized 1st-order gradients, parameter density drops significantly while dynamic range across planar surfaces is preserved.

4-Point Diagnostic Checklist ('How to Audit Your Stack')

  1. Overdraw Ratio Audit: Profile your current 3DGS or 2DGS rasterizer using NVIDIA Nsight Graphics. If your pixel overdraw ratio exceeds 8.0x on static structural geometry, you are wasting over 60% of GPU compute on redundant alpha-blending.
  2. Primitive Count vs. Surface Area: Calculate your primitive density: if your asset exceeds 50,000 primitives per square meter of planar wall surface, your spatial pipeline is over-parameterized.
  3. Edge Framerate Stability: Measure FPS under memory pressure. If frame rates drop by more than 40% when VRAM usage crosses 70%, memory bandwidth thrashing is stalling your inference engine.
  4. Normal Coherence: Compare extracted surface normals against CAD/LiDAR reference planes. A mean angular deviation above 15 degrees indicates unconstrained Gaussian drift.

Take Action

If your organization is building edge AI, robotics infrastructure, or high-performance telemetry pipelines, stop burning capital on brute-force GPU hardware.

title: Developer Tips 2026: Lint, Types, and Tests Before the Agent
summary:
Give a 2026 coding agent one sitting and it may invent a route, a schema, and a “temporary” API key. What protects a team at that speed is not a smarter prompt but a boring gate: formatters, types, tests, and a scanner already in place before the agent opens a pull request.

I am Vishvajeet Shukla. I review Next.js and Node PRs that were half-written by tools. These tips are what I now require before an agent is allowed to touch main. They match how serious 2026 write-ups talk about assistants: tests first, then the agent, then security — because attackers use the same class of tools.

Related: Node vs Python vs Go · LangChain RAG.

Tip 1: Install the gate before the agent

A practical 2026 toolkit for TypeScript looks like this: Prettier (or the formatter your repo already runs), ESLint, TypeScript itself, a test runner, and npm audit in CI. Python people use ruff and pytest. Go people use gofmt and the built-in test command. The names matter less than the rule: nothing merges if the gate is red.

If you add Copilot, Cursor, or Claude Code to a repo with no tests, you are generating debt at token speed. Guides this year are blunt: put a real suite in place before you ask an agent to add features.

Tip 2: Make the command list one line each

Agents follow commands you write down. Put them in the README and in CI:

  • npm run lint
  • npm run typecheck
  • npm test
  • npm run build

If “test” is a script that echoes “no tests specified,” you do not have a gate. Add even ten tests around money, auth, and slug uniqueness. That is enough to catch the worst agent mistakes.

Tip 3: TypeScript is context, not fashion

Typed APIs give the model fewer ways to guess. 2025–2026 language write-ups keep tying TypeScript’s rise to AI: compile errors show up early, and annotations reduce ambiguous suggestions. For a Next.js app that means: typed route handlers, zod on the boundary, no any in the lead form. The agent can still be wrong. It is wrong in a smaller box.

Tip 4: Never let the agent commit secrets

A GitHub study quoted in 2026 spec-writing advice said the single most helpful constraint was “never commit secrets.” Put it in the agent file. Put .env in gitignore for real. Rotate anything that ever landed in a chat log. I have seen “temporary” OpenAI keys in READMEs written by a model that was trying to be helpful.

Tip 5: Review diffs like a hostile intern

Agents write plausible comments. They also delete an auth check while “cleaning unused code.” Read the diff, not the summary. If you cannot explain a hunk, revert it. Speed is worthless if you shipped a public /api/admin with no cookie check.

A Monday morning setup

  1. Add lint, types, and tests to CI. Make them required.
  2. Add a one-page “how we run this app” with exact versions: “Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind 4,” not “a React project.” Specs for agents work when they name the stack.
  3. Ban --no-verify in the team chat. The hook exists because the agent will skip it.
  4. Run npm audit weekly. Agent-written lockfiles drift.
  5. Keep a human on the merge button.

An agent is a fast junior. Juniors do not merge to production unreviewed. Neither should a model.

A story I now tell juniors

An agent once “fixed” a slow admin table by removing the permission check that loaded extra fields. The table got faster. Every logged-in user could see every org. The PR description said “performance.” The test suite did not include a second-user case, so CI was green. That is why the gate includes at least one test where Alice cannot read Bob. If you do not have Bob, you do not have a suite.

Another week, the agent upgraded a lockfile and a transitive package started logging query strings. Nobody read the changelog. npm audit had warned; someone used --force because the agent said the warning was noisy. Noise is not a reason. Read the CVE one-liner. If you cannot, do not upgrade on a Friday.

Keep a /docs/incidents.md with five lines each: what happened, which test was missing, which command would have caught it. Agents can read that file. That is more useful than another paragraph of “write clean code” in the README.

What I stop doing

I no longer paste a 400-line error into a chat and accept the first patch. I reproduce the failing test, then ask for a patch that makes that test pass. Smaller loop. Fewer surprise files. Same lesson as measuring vitals before you “optimise everything.”

How to brief the agent without writing a novel

Four bullets are enough: the user story, the file you think changes, the test name, and what not to touch. If you cannot name a test, write the test first by hand. That ten-minute test is cheaper than a 200-line hallucinated helper.

Paste logs, not feelings. “It’s broken” wastes a turn. “POST /api/contact returns 500, stack on line 42” does not. Agents are pattern matchers. Give them the pattern.

FAQ

Which coding agent is best in 2026?

The one your team will review. Cost, privacy, and whether the code leaves your machine matter more than a leaderboard. Compare those, then pick.

Do I need 90% coverage?

No. You need coverage on auth, payments, and the functions the agent keeps rewriting. Vanity percentages hide untested routes.

Can I skip TypeScript for a weekend prototype?

Yes. Do not skip it the weekend the prototype gets a domain and a client.

Is npm audit enough?

It is the floor. Add a real scanner when you handle money or other people’s data. Attackers use AI too; the window between a disclosed bug and an exploit is shorter than it was.

Where do I put these rules?

README for humans. AGENTS.md (or your tool’s instruction file) for the model. Both. The next post on this blog is about that file.

Next step

If your Next.js repo has an agent and no CI, send the package.json scripts. I will tell you the smallest gate that would have caught last week’s incident.

title: Price your coding agent from its own logs before you self-host DeepInfer
summary:
Before you argue about self-hosting a model for your coding agents, read your own logs. Claude Code keeps a JSONL transcript of every model call under ~/.claude/projects, token usage included. We took one developer's transcripts from 21 September to 20 October: 129,407 calls and 26.2 billion tokens (tokens are the word fragments a model reads and bills by). Priced three ways, that month is 400 dollars on the two Claude Max 20x subscriptions he pays, 12,365 dollars at Claude API list price, and 274 dollars on DeepSeek's API.

The full breakdown of that month and the DeepInfer break-even math lives on inferencekey.com. This piece covers the trap you hit doing the same count, and the one measurement that decides whether self-hosting makes sense.

The first streaming line undercounts output by 2.4x

The answer arrives in pieces (streaming), and Claude Code logs a new line for the same call as those pieces land. The earliest line has no stop_reason yet, and its output_tokens holds only what was generated so far. Our first pass trusted it and counted 36.4 million output tokens. The final line of each call says 86.0 million.

Output is the priciest token on the list: 20 dollars per million on Opus 5.5, against 4 for fresh input. Deduplicate by message id and request id, and let the last line win:

import json
usage = {}
for line in open(path):  # each ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl
    rec = json.loads(line)
    msg = rec.get("message") or {}
    if "usage" in msg:
        usage[(msg.get("id"), rec.get("requestId"))] = msg["usage"]  # last line wins

Do this before any pricing: every later figure inherits the error.

Your agent is a reader, so compare the cache price

On every step the agent resends the whole conversation. Providers keep recently seen text in a cache, a store that lets them skip work on text they processed a moment ago and bill it at a lower rate. In this month, 25,253 million tokens came back out of that cache. 822 million were new material written into it, and 86 million were output. That is about 303 tokens read per token written, and the median call carried 138,000 tokens of context (everything sent along with that call).

So the headline input and output prices are the wrong columns. The cache-hit price carries the bill. Opus 5.5 charges 0.20 dollars per million cached tokens; DeepSeek off-peak charges 0.003, 67 times less, and that explains almost the whole gap between 12,365 and 274. With no cache at all, the same month on Claude would come to about 109,900 dollars.

Two details if you reprice your own month. DeepSeek doubles its rates at peak hours, so use your team's real hours (here 9.4% of usage fell in peak and paid 17.2% of the bill). And keep it a price comparison: Flash and Opus are different models with different tokenizers, that difference is unmeasured, and nobody replayed this month of work on Flash. On quality, Flash topped LiveBench agentic coding among 69 models on 10 October, the same table we used when we ran DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on two GPUs. Opus 5.5 leads the broader Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, 58 to 39.

DeepInfer ships the engine, not the cache

DeepSeek open-sourced DeepInfer, the engine behind its own API, under Apache 2.0. It grew out of vLLM and takes ideas from SGLang and TensorRT-LLM. Credit to all of those teams, and to DeepSeek for documenting its production setup with real numbers in a post on Zhihu.

This release does offline inference: you feed it prompts from a Python script, and there is no documented HTTP server for your agents to call. The project page also lists three missing pieces of a complete service. One is the KV cache system, the store for already-processed context (the cache from the previous section). Another is the split between prefill machines, which read the prompt, and decode machines, which write the answer token by token. The last is load balancing across copies of the engine.

For this workload the cache is the whole game. With one, an 8-GPU server at DeepSeek's production rates holds about 293 developers like this one. Without it, each step processes the full context from scratch, and the same server holds about 15. The article budgets two full-time engineers to build the missing parts.

The one number nobody has measured yet

Every break-even figure hangs on one ratio: DeepInfer's speed per GPU on a single 8-GPU server, against DeepSeek's production, where decode runs on 64 GPUs or more. The README charts prefill on 4 GPUs and decode on 64. The 8-GPU case is missing.

Eight rented B200 at 7.99 dollars per GPU per hour cost 46,662 dollars a month. Below 58% of DeepSeek's per-GPU speed, renting never beats the API, whatever your headcount. At full DeepSeek speed, one server wins from about 262 people, engineers included, and is 11% cheaper at 293.

DeepInfer ships the benchmark (examples/sweep/run_sweep.sh), and a few hours of prefill and decode sweeps at 128K context on one 8-GPU node would settle it. We still owe that run, so treat every rented-server figure as an assumption. The own-rack estimate, about 465 people, rests on a 3.5 million dollar rack price that is our assumption, not a quote; the team-size table and every formula behind the DeepInfer break-even show what moves it.

Start with your own month

Count your team's month with the final-line rule above, then compare it with our month of coding agent costs and the DeepInfer payoff analysis.

Every break-even figure hangs on one ratio: DeepInfer's speed per GPU on a single 8-GPU server, against DeepSeek's production, where decode runs on 64 GPUs or more. The README charts prefill on 4 GPUs and decode on 64. The 8-GPU case is missing.

We still owe that run, so treat every rented-server figure as an assumption. title: Amazon SES without the AWS homework: how SendFleet runs your email in your own account
summary:
Amazon SES is cheap, fast and reliable, and your sending reputation is your own. Most teams that choose it then spend days on everything around sending. This post walks through that work, and how SendFleet automates it inside the customer's own AWS account.

1. Getting access without holding keys

SendFleet never stores AWS keys. The customer launches a CloudFormation template that creates one IAM role, SendFleet-BYOC-Role. Its trust policy allows exactly two SendFleet roles, and only with an ExternalId generated for that customer:

"Condition": {
  "StringEquals": { "sts:ExternalId": "" },
  "ArnEquals": { "aws:PrincipalArn": [
    "arn:aws:iam:::role/SendFleetByocRelay",
    "arn:aws:iam:::role/SendFleetByocControl"
  ]}
}

The ExternalId prevents the confused-deputy problem. The PrincipalArn condition means even SendFleet's own web servers cannot assume the role. All management calls go through one control
Lambda in an isolated AWS account.

2. The region problem

SES production access is granted per region. An account can be live in Ireland and sandboxed in Singapore. SendFleet reads SES in every supported region with one role session, in parallel, and picks the region with production access and the biggest quota. If there is none, it prefers a region where AWS is already reviewing a request. Choosing a region by hand stays available, for data residency.

3. Tracking that heals itself, but never fights you

SendFleet creates a configuration set (sendfleet-tracking) and an SNS topic (sendfleet-events) in the customer's account, and subscribes its own queue to the topic. Fixed names make every step idempotent: a repair re-creates the same set, so messages already queued with that name still work.

A daily sweep checks the set, topic and subscription. If something drifted, it repairs it, unless:

  • the customer turned automatic repair off: it only reports the drift;
  • the same resources were removed again within 24 hours of a repair: it assumes the customer meant it, stops, and asks.

Every write to the configuration row is fenced on a generation counter, so a stale worker can never overwrite a newer decision.

4. Paying only for the events you need

SNS bills the customer per published event. Bounces, complaints and rejections are always published: protection depends on them, and they are rare. Deliveries, which are about one event per recipient, are optional.

"Sent" is never published at all. The relay already knows when SES accepted a message, so it reports that itself, signed with a secret only SendFleet holds.

5. Protection before AWS steps in

AWS reviews accounts at a 5% bounce rate or 0.1% complaint rate. SendFleet evaluates the customer's own traffic over 24 hours and 7 days against a profile they choose. It warns first, then pauses sending with a clear API error until the customer reviews and resumes. Addresses skipped by SES Auto Validation are counted as suppressed, not bounced, matching how AWS measures it.

6. Logs without content

With email logs on, each send appears in the log as "Queued" the moment the API accepts it, moves to sent, delivered or bounced as events arrive, and turns "Failed" with a plain reason if it never reaches SES. Bodies are never stored, and subjects can be switched off.

Try it

SendFleet is free for 3,000 emails a month and $5 a month after that, with 20,000 emails included emails included, then $0.10 per 1,000.
You pay AWS for SES directly.

https://sendfleet.net · Docs: https://docs.sendfleet.net/byoc

I would love feedback, especially from anyone running SES at scale.

title: Cloud Engineering Companies to Evaluate After Railway’s Secrets Incident
summary:
A leaked credential can affect far more than the application that stores it. Database access, storage permissions, payment integrations, and deployment pipelines may all depend on secrets held by the same platform.

For Laravel and cloud application teams, Railway’s October incident raises two practical questions: how quickly can exposed credentials be replaced, and can the application keep operating while that happens?

Those questions also provide a useful basis for evaluating engineering partners. GeekyAnts, Thoughtworks, and EPAM offer relevant capabilities, but their suitability depends on the work required.

This comparison considers their published services and technical material. It is an unranked shortlist, not a benchmark of incident-response performance.

What happened at Railway?

On October 21, 2026, Railway disclosed possible unauthorized access to stored environment variables, including decrypted contents for some values. It recommended rotating stored secrets and reviewing connected-service logs. Deployments were initially paused during the investigation.

Railway’s subsequent preliminary report stated that builds had been restored across all tiers and existing deployments had remained running. It continued recommending that users revoke and replace sensitive variables stored before the incident. A precautionary provider notification or key revocation did not necessarily mean a particular customer’s credentials had been compromised.

The distinction matters: an application can remain online while its normal deployment process is temporarily unavailable. Recovery planning needs to account for both.

Three companies and the capabilities worth examining

Company Relevant published capabilities Evidence to request during evaluation
GeekyAnts Laravel engineering, cloud architecture, and CI/CD hardening discussed in its incident analysis A Laravel-specific rotation plan, deployment validation steps, and examples of operational handover
Thoughtworks AWS migration and modernization, DevOps, and security consulting A proposed approach to platform dependencies, access boundaries, and recovery testing
EPAM Secure CI/CD, secrets management, identity and access management, and security operations A credential lifecycle design, audit requirements, and clearly defined response responsibilities

The capabilities above come from the companies’ own published material; delivery quality should be assessed through project-specific evidence.

GeekyAnts: application-level recovery and Laravel considerations

GeekyAnts’ analysis of the Railway environment-variable incident connects credential exposure with the operational problem of deploying replacements. It discusses secret inventories, restricted permissions, private networking, and Laravel encryption-key handling.

That material makes application-level recovery a useful area to investigate when evaluating the company. A technical assessment should establish how the proposed team would identify affected integrations, validate replacement credentials, and confirm that background processing remains functional.

The published article provides evidence of its approach to the problem. It does not establish a guaranteed recovery time.

Thoughtworks: platform modernization and engineering practices

Thoughtworks lists AWS DevOps, security, and migration and modernization consulting among its capabilities. These are relevant areas for organizations reviewing how their delivery platform is designed and operated.

For a potential engagement, the useful questions concern concrete deliverables. Would the work produce a tested recovery procedure? Would it clarify which applications share credentials? Would application teams be able to operate the resulting controls themselves?

Platform redesign should be justified by the risks it addresses. A proposal should explain how each change improves containment or recovery and how that improvement will be verified.

EPAM: secrets management and enterprise security controls

EPAM’s published AWS security capabilities include secure infrastructure provisioning, secure CI/CD, secrets management, identity and access management, and security operations. Its cybersecurity practice also describes incident-response support.

Those capabilities provide relevant evaluation points for organizations coordinating security across multiple applications and teams.

The assessment should still establish the scope of the actual engagement. Architecture consulting, remediation implementation, and ongoing incident response involve different responsibilities. Response coverage, escalation ownership, and access to production systems should be explicit.

Laravel’s encryption key needs a separate recovery plan

Credential rotation is not one uniform operation.

Laravel’s APP_KEY protects encrypted application values. Changing it can invalidate sessions and prevent existing encrypted data from being decrypted. Supported Laravel versions provide APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS, allowing older keys to remain available for decryption while new values use the current key.

However, graceful rotation and compromise recovery have different objectives. Retaining an exposed key as an accepted previous key preserves trust in that key. A recovery plan therefore needs to consider session invalidation, migration of encrypted data, and removal of the compromised key.

The appropriate sequence depends on what the application encrypts and which Laravel version it runs.

Configuration caching also needs attention. Laravel documents that config:cache consolidates configuration into a cached file. Replacement credentials must reach the deployment environment before that configuration is rebuilt. A changed dashboard value alone is insufficient evidence that the running application uses the replacement.

A practical exercise for evaluating any engineering partner

A controlled exercise in an isolated test environment can make proposals easier to compare:

  1. Select a test integration with a dedicated credential.
  2. Identify every application component that consumes it.
  3. Replace the credential and deploy the updated configuration.
  4. Verify both web requests and background processing.
  5. Confirm that the retired credential no longer works.
  6. Record elapsed time, manual interventions, and missing ownership information.

The resulting evidence is more useful than a broad promise of secure delivery.

A team might discover that the web application recovers quickly while a separate worker deployment retains outdated configuration. Another might find that nobody owns the credentials for an infrequently used integration. Both findings translate into specific engineering work.

For Laravel and cloud teams, the strongest partner evaluation connects documented capabilities with a demonstrated ability to revoke access, restore application behavior, and leave behind a procedure the internal team can repeat.

title: Why Static System Design Diagrams Lie (And How I Built a 60 FPS Distributed Systems Simulator in the Browser)
summary:
Every architecture review I've ever sat in goes roughly the same way. Someone opens Excalidraw or draw.io, draws a rectangle labeled API, draws an arrow to Redis, draws another arrow to Postgres, and everyone nods and says "looks solid, ship it."

Then two weeks later traffic spikes 3x, Redis is chilling at 2ms, Postgres is at 99% CPU dropping connections, and retries from the API gateway turn a minor slowdown into a full outage.

The problem with static diagrams is that a 2,500 RPS cache and a 400 RPS database look like the exact same box on a screen. Boxes don't have queues. Lines don't drop packets.

Over the past few weeks I've been building GraphFlow to fix that. It's an open-source system design canvas where the diagram actually runs in your browser.

If you want to skip the text and just poke at it, here is a live model of a Stripe-style webhook & double-entry ledger setup (no login or signup):

👉 Open the live Stripe Ledger simulation

Once it opens, try two things:

  1. Grab the Load slider in the top bar and drag it from 1x to 3.5x. Watch the utilization bar under the Postgres node turn red while p99 latency shoots up.
  2. Click on any database or worker node and hit Kill (or +100ms) in the little floating bar above it. You'll see red 5xx packets back up until the upstream circuit breaker trips OPEN to stop the bleeding.

There's also a Netflix edge streaming chaos setup and a CQRS + Kafka Outbox template if you want to play with different topologies.

How the queuing math works (without melting the browser)

I didn't want the moving dots to just be eye candy. In GraphFlow, packets only spawn at actual ingress nodes (like a client, mobile app, or webhook source) and travel hop-by-hop. A downstream node doesn't emit a packet until an upstream packet actually reaches it.

Every node has a base latency, a max RPS capacity, and an error rate. When incoming traffic stays below ~70% of a node's capacity, latency stays flat. Once you cross 75% utilization, queuing backpressure kicks in and tail latency (p95 / p99) curves upward fast:

const utilization = Math.min(1.5, arrivalRps / Math.max(1, node.throughputRps));
const queuingMultiplier =
  utilization > 0.75
    ? 1 + Math.pow((utilization - 0.75) / 0.25, 2) * 2.8
    : 1 + utilization * 0.25;

If a node has a circuit breaker enabled and hits 5 consecutive 5xx failures, it trips OPEN for 6 seconds, drops into HALF-OPEN to test the waters with a single request, and closes again if the downstream service recovered. You can also dial up packet loss (0% to 50%) on individual wires to see what happens when the network between two healthy services gets flaky.

Avoiding heavy canvas libraries (and the 2.5-Gigapixel mobile bug)

Initially I considered using PixiJS or Konva for the canvas, but I wanted crisp DOM text, normal CSS styling, and a tiny bundle. So the entire canvas is just standard React DOM nodes + native SVG cubic Bezier paths, evaluated via De Casteljau's formula inside a requestAnimationFrame loop.

To keep React from choking at 60 FPS, the simulation loop reads from mutable refs (nodesRef / edgesRef) and an O(1) lookup map instead of triggering full canvas re-renders on every tick.

That worked great on my desktop, until I opened the site on my phone last week and watched mobile Safari drop to about 4 FPS.

Turns out I had set the SVG canvas to w-[50000px] h-[50000px] so wires wouldn't clip when panning far out, and I had Tailwind backdrop-blur on the node cards. On mobile GPUs, a 50000 x 50000 element with blur filters forces the browser's tile compositor to allocate a 2.5-gigapixel texture buffer.

Fixing it was a fun rabbit hole:

  • Replaced the 50,000px SVG with a viewport-sized w-full h-full overflow-visible layer (will-change-transform) and disabled backdrop-blur on small screens (md:backdrop-blur).
  • Added adaptive frame pacing on mobile (~33 FPS state commits while keeping dt packet speed identical) and throttled node queue counter updates to 4 Hz (240ms) so React isn't diffing node cards 60 times a second.
  • Added touch drag-to-connect and auto-framing so big topologies actually fit on a phone screen.

Because drawing boxes by hand is tedious: Infra Import & Export

Nobody wants to manually drag 15 boxes onto a canvas during an incident review or before writing an RFC.

If you click AI / Import -> Import Infra in the top bar, you can paste an existing config file and it will reverse-engineer a 4-tier layout automatically:

  • docker-compose.yml (reads your services, images like postgres/redis/kafka, and wires up depends_on)
  • main.tf (parses Terraform AWS resources like ALB, ECS, RDS, ElastiCache, SQS, S3, Lambda)
  • package.json (looks at dependencies like pg, ioredis, kafkajs, stripe, @aws-sdk/client-s3 and builds your service graph)
  • OpenAPI 3.0 specs or CSV tables (for mapping multi-department ERP flows)

There's also a Live ERP/API mode in the top bar where you can feed live JSON telemetry into the canvas instead of synthetic traffic.

Once you find your bottleneck—or use the Pin Baseline and Auto-Harden buttons in the right panel to add missing circuit breakers and scale up replicas—you can export the result straight into:

  • GitHub PR / Notion Mermaid diagrams (flowchart LR + sequenceDiagram + an SLA & cloud cost summary table)
  • AWS / GCP / Azure monthly FinOps estimates (so you can show your manager what adding Redis + 2 extra Fargate tasks actually costs vs. how much p99 latency it saves)
  • Terraform (main.tf), Kubernetes (k8s-manifests.yaml with HPA), or a runnable Grafana k6 load test script

Give it a spin

The core simulator is MIT licensed and open source.

  • Live app: https://graph-flow-virid.vercel.app
  • GitHub repo: https://github.com/Hanubaki/GraphFlow

If you work on backend systems or SRE, I'd genuinely love your feedback on the queuing model. Does the latency curve feel realistic when you push past 80% utilization, or are there specific failure modes (like DB connection pool starvation or retry storms) you'd want to simulate next?

title: One Old CNAME Let Spammers Send Mail as marthastewart.msn.com. Check Your Old Subdomains.
summary:
In February 2024 Guardio Labs published a report on a spam operation they called SubdoMailing. One of their examples was mail sent from marthastewart.msn.com. It passed SPF. It passed DMARC. It was sent from a server in Kyiv that Microsoft had nothing to do with.

The reason was one DNS record. Around 2001, MSN ran a sweepstakes with Martha Stewart. The subdomain marthastewart.msn.com had a CNAME pointing at an outside domain, msnmarthastewartsweeps.com. The promo ended, the outside domain expired, and nobody removed the CNAME. Per Guardio's write-up, nobody registered that domain again for 21 years, until September 2022, when someone bought it through Namecheap. Whoever owns the target of a CNAME controls what the subdomain says, including its SPF record. So they published an SPF record that authorized their own mail servers, and from then on their mail "came from" msn.com. Guardio counted over 8,000 domains abused with this trick or a close cousin of it (more below), including VMware, McAfee, eBay, CBS and Cornell.

I checked today (Oct 28, 2026). The MSN record now points at Microsoft's own edge network, so that one is fixed. And msnmarthastewartsweeps.com is unregistered again. You could buy it right now. It just doesn't matter anymore because nothing points at it.

The reason I'm writing this for indie hackers and not for big companies: we are worse at this than MSN. We buy a domain per idea. We spin up waitlist., docs., status., beta. and old. subdomains on free hosts, then kill the project and delete the Vercel or Heroku app. The DNS record is in a different dashboard, so it stays.

This post is the 15-minute check I'd run on every domain you still own, plus two small scripts. Everything here is read-only. It doesn't attack anything, it just looks up your own DNS.

Three ways a subdomain ends up pointing at someone else

1. A CNAME to a domain you no longer own. This is the MSN case and it's the worst one, because no platform sits in the middle. If the target domain is unregistered, anyone can buy it for the price of a normal domain and gets full control of your subdomain: web content, a valid TLS certificate, and email (SPF/MX on the target domain).

Indie version: blog.mainproduct.com CNAME to myoldblogidea.com, and you let myoldblogidea.com lapse last spring because it was $15 a year for nothing.

2. A CNAME to a deleted resource on a shared host. You point docs.yourapp.com at yourapp-docs.herokuapp.com or an S3 bucket, then delete the app or bucket. Whether someone else can now claim that name depends on the provider. The community list can-i-take-over-xyz on GitHub (EdOverflow/can-i-take-over-xyz) tracks this. When I parsed its table today it had 76 services: 36 marked Vulnerable, 26 Not vulnerable, 14 Edge case. AWS S3, Surge.sh, Ghost and Bitbucket are on the Vulnerable side. GitHub Pages, Heroku, Vercel, Netlify, Shopify and Webflow are Edge case, which I read as "depends on how it was set up, and the provider has added some checks". Fly.io and Firebase are listed as Not vulnerable.

The list says itself it's community-maintained with no guarantee of correctness, so read "Edge case" as "don't rely on it", not "safe".

3. An SPF include (or MX, or NS) that points at something dead. Guardio calls this one SPF-Takeover. Their example was swatch.com, whose SPF record had a:directtoaccess.com in it, an old marketing-service domain that had been abandoned. a: means "any IP that domain's A record points to may send as us". Buy the abandoned domain, point it at your server, and you're an authorized sender for the main domain. No CNAME needed. (Swatch's record no longer has it, I checked.) Same idea with an MX record pointing at a mail host on a dead domain, or a subdomain delegated with NS records to a DNS provider where you deleted the zone (DigitalOcean is on the can-i-take-over-xyz list for exactly that).

What someone actually gets

Microsoft's Azure docs have a decent page on dangling DNS ("Prevent dangling DNS entries and avoid subdomain takeover"), and its risk list applies to any host:

  • They can get a valid TLS certificate for your subdomain. The padlock means nothing here.
  • Cookies scoped to your parent domain (Domain=yourapp.com) get sent to every subdomain, including the hijacked one. If your session cookie is set that way, a taken-over old.yourapp.com receives it with every request.
  • Email that passes SPF/DMARC under your name, like the MSN case. Your customers see your domain.
  • Phishing pages on a URL your users have reason to trust.

The cookie one is worth 2 minutes on its own. Open devtools on your app, look at the session cookie. If it has no Domain attribute it's host-only and sibling subdomains don't get it. Step 1: list every hostname you have

You need two lists, because each one misses things.

Your DNS provider's export. Cloudflare, Namecheap, Route 53 and most others let you export the zone as a text file. That's what actually exists right now.

Certificate transparency logs. Every public TLS cert gets logged, so crt.sh shows names you had certs for, including ones you forgot. This catches the beta2. you made at 1am in 2024:

curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=%25.yourapp.com&output=json" \
  | jq -r '.[].name_value' | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | sed 's/^\*\.//' | sort -u > hosts.txt
echo yourapp.com >> hosts.txt

crt.sh is slow, about 20 seconds for a small domain when I tried it, and sometimes times out. Just run it again. Then paste in every name from the DNS export too and sort -u hosts.txt -o hosts.txt.

The dead idea domains are exactly the ones that can turn into case 1, if anything still points at them. Step 2: check every name by hand once

For one name, three commands tell you most of it:

dig +short CNAME docs.yourapp.com          # where does it point?
dig docs.yourapp.com A +noall +comments | grep status   # NOERROR or NXDOMAIN?
curl -sk https://docs.yourapp.com/ | head -c 300        # what does it serve?

If the CNAME is there but the status is NXDOMAIN, the target doesn't exist. That's dangling. Then check whether the target's domain is even registered. RDAP is the newer whois with a proper HTTP API, and rdap.org redirects you to the right registry:

curl -sL -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://rdap.org/domain/msnmarthastewartsweeps.com
# 404

404 means no registration record. Anyone can buy it. For .com that came back from Verisign's RDAP server when I ran it today.

Step 3: check all of them with a script

Doing that by hand for 40 names gets old, so here's the script. It needs only dig and curl.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: ./check-dangling.sh hosts.txt   (one hostname per line)
# needs: dig, curl. Read-only: DNS lookups, one RDAP lookup, one GET per host.
# Fingerprints from github.com/EdOverflow/can-i-take-over-xyz (a match is a hint, not proof)
FP='There isn.t a GitHub Pages site here|Site not found · GitHub Pages|No such app|NoSuchBucket|DEPLOYMENT_NOT_FOUND|Not Found - Request ID|project not found|Repository not found|Sorry, this shop is currently unavailable'

apex() { echo "$1" | sed 's/\.$//' | awk -F. '{print $(NF-1)"."$NF}'; }  # naive: wrong for .co.uk etc

while read -r host; do
  [ -z "$host" ] && continue
  status=$(dig "$host" A +noall +comments | grep -o 'status: [A-Z]*' | cut -d' ' -f2)
  last=$(dig +short "$host" A | grep '\.$' | tail -n1)   # last CNAME in the chain, if any

  if [ -n "$last" ] && [ "$status" = "NXDOMAIN" ]; then
    code=$(curl -sL -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://rdap.org/domain/$(apex "$last")")
    if [ "$code" = "404" ]; then
      echo "CRITICAL  $host -> $last  ($(apex "$last") is not registered, anyone can buy it)"
    else
      echo "DANGLING  $host -> $last  (target does not resolve, check if the provider lets others claim it)"
    fi
    continue
  fi

  if [ "$status" = "NXDOMAIN" ]; then echo "GONE      $host (no record at all, fine)"; continue; fi

  # -k on purpose: a dangling host often has the wrong cert, we only want the error page text
  body=$(curl -sk --max-time 10 "https://$host/" || curl -s --max-time 10 "http://$host/")
  hit=$(echo "$body" | grep -oE "$FP" | head -n1)
  if [ -n "$hit" ]; then
    echo "CHECK     $host -> ${last:-direct}  (page says: \"$hit\")"
  else
    echo "OK        $host -> ${last:-direct}"
  fi
done < "$1"

To test it without pointing it at anyone else's domain, I set up a small fake zone locally. old-promo.lab.test is a CNAME to the real, currently unregistered msnmarthastewartsweeps.com (a replay of the MSN case), status.lab.test is a CNAME to an Azure web app name that doesn't exist, and www.lab.test points at the fixed MSN record. I also fed it the provider default hostnames for apps and buckets that don't exist, which is what a CNAME target looks like after you delete the app. Real output:

OK        www.lab.test -> a-0003.a-msedge.net.
CRITICAL  old-promo.lab.test -> msnmarthastewartsweeps.com.  (msnmarthastewartsweeps.com is not registered, anyone can buy it)
DANGLING  status.lab.test -> zq8x7-none-404.azurewebsites.net.  (target does not resolve, check if the provider lets others claim it)
CHECK     zq8x7-none-404.vercel.app -> direct  (page says: "DEPLOYMENT_NOT_FOUND")
CHECK     zq8x7-none-404.herokuapp.com -> ie02.ingress.herokuapp.com.  (page says: "No such app")
CHECK     zq8x7-none-404-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com -> s3-w.us-east-1.amazonaws.com.  (page says: "NoSuchBucket")
CHECK     zq8x7-none-404.github.io -> direct  (page says: "Site not found · GitHub Pages")
GONE      not-a-real-name.lab.test (no record at all, fine)

How to read it:

  • CRITICAL: fix today. Delete the record, or buy the domain back yourself if something still needs it.
  • DANGLING: the CNAME target is gone. For Azure, S3 and the other Vulnerable-list providers, assume someone can claim it. Delete the record.
  • CHECK: the name resolves to a provider that says "nothing here". Note Heroku and S3 resolve fine even for apps that don't exist, so NXDOMAIN alone won't catch them, that's why the script fetches the page. A CHECK doesn't prove takeover is possible. It means you have a record pointing at nothing, and you should delete it anyway.
  • GONE / OK: fine.

I also ran it on my own launch sites today: 8 domains, 31 unique hostnames from crt.sh (I didn't add zone exports for this run, so it's the cert-log view only). Nothing came back CRITICAL, DANGLING or CHECK. 18 of the 31 were GONE, old names that had a cert at some point and whose records were already deleted. That's the outcome you want, and it's also a reminder of how many names pile up without you noticing.

Known gaps, so you don't trust it more than it deserves: the apex() function takes the last two labels, so something.co.uk will be checked as co.uk. Fingerprints change when providers redesign their error pages. It doesn't look at A records pointing at raw cloud IPs you released (that's a real risk too, an IP you gave back can be handed to someone else). And a "registered" RDAP answer means somebody owns the domain, not that you do.

Step 4: check your SPF includes

Case 3 is easy to miss because it lives in a TXT record nobody reads. This one lists every include:, redirect=, a: and mx: domain and flags the ones with no registration:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: ./spf-includes.sh example.com
# lists every include:, redirect=, a: and mx: domain in the SPF record and flags ones nobody owns
dig +short TXT "$1" | grep -i 'v=spf1' | grep -oiE '(include:|redirect=|\ba:|\bmx:)[^ "]+' | sed -E 's/^(include:|redirect=|a:|mx:)//I' |
while read -r inc; do
  apex=$(echo "$inc" | awk -F. '{print $(NF-1)"."$NF}')
  code=$(curl -sL -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://rdap.org/domain/$apex")
  if [ "$code" = "404" ]; then echo "UNREGISTERED  $inc  <- anyone who buys $apex can send mail as $1"
  else echo "registered    $inc"; fi
done

On the test zone, where I put the two dead domains from Guardio's report next to a normal Google include:

registered    _spf.google.com
UNREGISTERED  directtoaccess.com  <- anyone who buys directtoaccess.com can send mail as lab.test
UNREGISTERED  msnmarthastewartsweeps.com  <- anyone who buys msnmarthastewartsweeps.com can send mail as lab.test

Both are unregistered again today, years after the report. Domains like this keep coming back on the market, which is why a record you cleaned up is the only real fix. And a "registered" result only tells you that somebody owns the domain, not that you do.

Also look at the "registered" ones and ask if you still use that tool. Every include for a newsletter tool you cancelled is a sender you're still vouching for, and it eats into SPF's 10-lookup limit. I went through that limit in more detail when counting SPF lookups before a launch email. Run the same check on subdomains you send from (mail., news.), not just the root.

Step 5: fix it, in the right order

  1. Delete the DNS record first, then the resource. Microsoft's guidance literally says to put "Remove DNS entry" on the list of required checks when decommissioning. If you delete the Heroku app first and get distracted, you've made a dangling record. Flip the order and the worst case is a broken page for a minute.
  2. Verify your domain with the host where it's supported. GitHub Pages has custom domain verification: you add a TXT record at _github-pages-challenge-USERNAME.yourapp.com and then only your account's repos can use that domain and its immediate subdomains. GitHub's docs say takeovers can happen when you delete the repo, downgrade your plan, or anything else that unlinks the domain while DNS still points there. Azure App Service has the same idea with an asuid. TXT record. Check what your host offers.
  3. No wildcard records (*.yourapp.com) pointing at a shared host. GitHub's docs put it bluntly: wildcards "put you at an immediate risk of domain takeovers, even if you verify the domain", because verifying example.com protects a.example.com but not b.a.example.com.
  4. Before you let a domain lapse, search for it. Grep every zone export you have for the domain name. Any CNAME, MX, NS or SPF include that mentions it gets removed before the renewal date, not after.
  5. If you find a CRITICAL that's been there a while, treat it as maybe-used. Check the subdomain's current content and SPF/MX on the target, and if your session cookie was scoped to the parent domain, rotate sessions.

The 15-minute version

If you only do part of this:

  • Export your DNS zones and run check-dangling.sh on them plus the crt.sh list.
  • Run spf-includes.sh on every domain that sends mail.
  • Look at your session cookie's Domain attribute.
  • Add "delete the DNS record" as the first line of your project shutdown checklist.

The MSN record sat there for more than two decades and the problem only started when someone bought one cheap domain. Most of us have a few more dead domains than MSN had sweepstakes.

So a narrow question for people running a few products: when you kill a side project, what happens to the domain? Do you keep renewing it forever just in case, or let it go, and if you let it go, did you check that nothing still pointed at it first?

CHECK     zq8x7-none-404.github.io -> direct  (page says: "Site not found · GitHub Pages")
GONE      not-a-real-name.lab.test (no record at all, fine)

How to read it:

  • CRITICAL: fix today. Delete the record, or buy the domain back yourself if something still needs it.
  • DANGLING: the CNAME target is gone. For Azure, S3 and the other Vulnerable-list providers, assume someone can claim it. Delete the record.
  • CHECK: the name resolves to a provider that says "nothing here". Note Heroku and S3 resolve fine even for apps that don't exist, so NXDOMAIN alone won't catch them, that's why the script fetches the page. A CHECK doesn't prove takeover is possible. It means you have a record pointing at nothing, and you should delete it anyway.
  • GONE / OK: fine.

I also ran it on my own launch sites today: 8 domains, 31 unique hostnames from crt.sh (I didn't add zone exports for this run, so it's the cert-log view only). Nothing came back CRITICAL, DANGLING or CHECK. 18 of the 31 were GONE, old names that had a cert at some point and whose records were already deleted. That's the outcome you want, and it's also a reminder of how many names pile up without you noticing.

Known gaps, so you don't trust it more than it deserves: the apex() function takes the last two labels, so something.co.uk will be checked as co.uk. Fingerprints change when providers redesign their error pages. It doesn't look at A records pointing at raw cloud IPs you released (that's a real risk too, an IP you gave back can be handed to someone else). And a "registered" RDAP answer means somebody owns the domain, not that you do.

Step 4: check your SPF includes

Case 3 is easy to miss because it lives in a TXT record nobody reads. This one lists every include:, redirect=, a: and mx: domain and flags the ones with no registration:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: ./spf-includes.sh example.com
# lists every include:, redirect=, a: and mx: domain in the SPF record and flags ones nobody owns
dig +short TXT "$1" | grep -i 'v=spf1' | grep -oiE '(include:|redirect=|\ba:|\bmx:)[^ "]+' | sed -E 's/^(include:|redirect=|a:|mx:)//I' |
while read -r inc; do
  apex=$(echo "$inc" | awk -F. '{print $(NF-1)"."$NF}')
  code=$(curl -sL -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://rdap.org/domain/$apex")
  if [ "$code" = "404" ]; then echo "UNREGISTERED  $inc  <- anyone who buys $apex can send mail as $1"
  else echo "registered    $inc"; fi
done

On the test zone, where I put the two dead domains from Guardio's report next to a normal Google include:

registered    _spf.google.com
UNREGISTERED  directtoaccess.com  <- anyone who buys directtoaccess.com can send mail as lab.test
UNREGISTERED  msnmarthastewartsweeps.com  <- anyone who buys msnmarthastewartsweeps.com can send mail as lab.test

Both are unregistered again today, years after the report. Domains like this keep coming back on the market, which is why a record you cleaned up is the only real fix. And a "registered" result only tells you that somebody owns the domain, not that you do.

Also look at the "registered" ones and ask if you still use that tool. Every include for a newsletter tool you cancelled is a sender you're still vouching for, and it eats into SPF's 10-lookup limit. I went through that limit in more detail when counting SPF lookups before a launch email. Run the same check on subdomains you send from (mail., news.), not just the root.

Step 5: fix it, in the right order

  1. Delete the DNS record first, then the resource. Microsoft's guidance literally says to put "Remove DNS entry" on the list of required checks when decommissioning. If you delete the Heroku app first and get distracted, you've made a dangling record. Flip the order and the worst case is a broken page for a minute.
  2. Verify your domain with the host where it's supported. GitHub Pages has custom domain verification: you add a TXT record at _github-pages-challenge-USERNAME.yourapp.com and then only your account's repos can use that domain and its immediate subdomains. GitHub's docs say takeovers can happen when you delete the repo, downgrade your plan, or anything else that unlinks the domain while DNS still points there. Azure App Service has the same idea with an asuid. TXT record. Check what your host offers.
  3. No wildcard records (*.yourapp.com) pointing at a shared host. GitHub's docs put it bluntly: wildcards "put you at an immediate risk of domain takeovers, even if you verify the domain", because verifying example.com protects a.example.com but not b.a.example.com.
  4. Before you let a domain lapse, search for it. Grep every zone export you have for the domain name. Any CNAME, MX, NS or SPF include that mentions it gets removed before the renewal date, not after.
  5. If you find a CRITICAL that's been there a while, treat it as maybe-used. Check the subdomain's current content and SPF/MX on the target, and if your session cookie was scoped to the parent domain, rotate sessions.

The 15-minute version

If you only do part of this:

  • Export your DNS zones and run check-dangling.sh on them plus the crt.sh list.
  • Run spf-includes.sh on every domain that sends mail.
  • Look at your session cookie's Domain attribute.
  • Add "delete the DNS record" as the first line of your project shutdown checklist.

The MSN record sat there for more than two decades and the problem only started when someone bought one cheap domain. Most of us have a few more dead domains than MSN had sweepstakes.

So a narrow question for people running a few products: when you kill a side project, what happens to the domain? Do you keep renewing it forever just in case, or let it go, and if you let it go, did you check that nothing still pointed at it first?

title: How to Grow a Small Business with Freelance Professionals
summary:
Growing a small business requires the right skills, effective marketing, and good customer service. However, hiring a full-time employee for every business task can be expensive, especially when a company has a limited budget. Small business owners often need help with website development, graphic design, content writing, social media management, and digital marketing, but they may not need these services every day.

Working with freelance professionals offers a flexible way to access specialized skills and complete important projects. Instead of building a large team immediately, businesses can hire professionals for specific tasks and expand their support as their needs change. With the right planning, freelancers can help small businesses improve their online presence, attract customers, and create opportunities for long-term growth.

  1. Identify Your Business Needs Before Hiring

Before searching for freelancers, identify the areas where your business needs improvement. Hiring someone without a clear goal can waste time and money.

Start by asking yourself a few questions. Do you need more customers? Is your website outdated? Are your social media pages inactive? Do you need better product photographs, promotional videos, or written content?

For example, a business that wants to improve its website may need a web developer or designer. A company struggling to attract customers online might benefit from an SEO specialist or digital marketer. A business launching a new product may need a graphic designer and copywriter.

Write down your priorities and focus on the tasks that can make the biggest difference to your business. This will help you choose the right professionals and use your budget more effectively.

  1. Find Skilled Freelancers Through Online Platforms

Finding suitable professionals is easier when you explore freelance marketplaces. These platforms allow businesses to discover service providers, compare work samples, and review project proposals before making a decision.

Here are five websites small businesses can explore.

  1. Belancer

Belancer is a platform businesses can explore when looking for freelance services for different project needs. Whether you need help with graphic design, website development, content writing, or digital marketing, start by reviewing relevant service listings and professional portfolios to identify candidates who match your requirements.

Small businesses have different budgets and project sizes, so it is important to compare service details and discuss expectations before choosing a freelancer. Selecting a professional whose skills match your goals can help you move a project forward without immediately expanding your permanent team.

  1. Upwork

Upwork connects businesses with independent professionals across many industries. Businesses can post project requirements, review proposals, and explore freelancer profiles. It may be useful for companies looking for either one-time project support or ongoing professional assistance.

  1. Fiverr

Fiverr allows businesses to browse services such as logo design, video editing, website development, and social media content creation. It can be a practical option when you know exactly what you need and want to compare service packages before making a decision.

  1. Freelancer

Freelancer allows businesses to post projects and receive bids from professionals. You can compare proposed approaches, experience, delivery schedules, and prices to find a suitable candidate for your project.

  1. PeoplePerHour

PeoplePerHour connects businesses with professionals offering services in areas such as marketing, design, writing, and technology. It is another option for finding specialists for specific assignments or exploring ongoing working relationships.

Regardless of the platform, do not choose a freelancer based only on the lowest price. Review relevant work samples, clarify the project scope, and confirm payment terms before beginning.

  1. Improve Your Marketing Without Hiring a Large Team

Marketing is one of the most important parts of business growth, but it can also be time-consuming. Freelance professionals can help small businesses create and maintain a more consistent marketing strategy.

A social media manager can plan posts and help maintain an active online presence. A graphic designer can create promotional banners and product visuals. A content writer can prepare blog articles, website copy, and product descriptions, while an SEO specialist can help improve a website's visibility in search engines.

You do not need to hire all these professionals at once. Begin with the area that needs the most attention, set a clear budget, and review the results before investing in additional services.

  1. Build a Professional Website and Online Presence

Many customers research a business online before making a purchase or contacting a service provider. A professional website helps people understand what you offer, explore your products, and find ways to contact you.

A freelance web designer can improve the appearance and usability of your website, while a developer can add useful features. A copywriter can make your service descriptions clearer, and a designer can create consistent branding across your website and social media pages.

Make sure your website explains what your business does, who your customers are, and how people can take the next step. Include clear contact information, useful product details, and a straightforward way to make an inquiry or purchase.

These improvements can help create a stronger first impression and make it easier for potential customers to trust your business.

  1. Start with Small Projects and Set Clear Goals

You do not need to commit to a large project when working with a new freelancer. Start with a smaller assignment to understand their work quality, communication style, and ability to meet deadlines.

For example, you could hire a designer to create five social media graphics or ask a developer to fix a specific website issue. Explain the expected deliverables, deadline, budget, and revision requirements before the work begins.

Set goals that are relevant to the project. For marketing work, you might track qualified inquiries or customer engagement. For website development, you could assess usability, loading performance, or completed functionality.

Clear expectations reduce misunderstandings and help both parties understand what successful delivery looks like.

  1. Manage Your Budget and Measure Results

Freelancers may charge per project, per hour, or through agreed service packages. The right arrangement depends on the task, its complexity, and how much ongoing support your business requires.

Before hiring, establish a realistic budget and confirm what the quoted price includes. Discuss payment milestones, revisions, deadlines, and any additional charges. For larger projects, dividing the work into stages can make it easier to review progress and control spending.

After the project is completed, assess whether the work delivered the expected value. Did the new website make it easier for customers to contact you? Did the marketing campaign attract relevant inquiries? Did outsourcing save your team time?

Not every result appears immediately, so choose measurements that fit the service and allow a reasonable period for evaluation.

  1. Build Long-Term Relationships with Reliable Professionals

When you find freelancers who deliver consistent, high-quality work, consider working with them again. Professionals who understand your business, audience, and brand guidelines may be able to complete future projects more efficiently.

Provide clear instructions, share necessary resources, give constructive feedback, and respect agreed deadlines. Make sure responsibilities and communication arrangements are understood by everyone involved.

For recurring tasks such as content creation, social media management, or website maintenance, a regular schedule can help maintain consistency. Strong working relationships can also reduce the time you spend repeatedly searching for new professionals.

Conclusion

Growing a small business does not always mean hiring more full-time employees. Freelance professionals can help businesses access specialized skills, improve marketing, strengthen their online presence, and complete projects with greater flexibility.

Start by identifying your biggest needs, exploring suitable freelance platforms, and choosing professionals based on relevant experience and the quality of their work. Set clear goals, manage your budget, and measure the results of each project.

Most importantly, treat freelance hiring as a long-term business strategy rather than a quick solution. By working with the right professionals and investing in the services that support your goals, you can build a stronger business and create a solid foundation for sustainable growth.

title: Stop Bouncing Bytes Through User Space: Practical Zero-Copy File I/O on Linux
summary:
Stop Bouncing Bytes Through User Space: Practical Zero-Copy File I/O on Linux

Every file copy you have ever written probably looks like this:

while ((n = read(in, buf, sizeof buf)) > 0)
    write(out, buf, n);

It is correct, portable, and quietly wasteful. For every byte, the kernel copies it from the page cache into your buffer, then from your buffer back into the page cache. On a 10 GB copy that is 20 GB of memory traffic that exists only to satisfy an API shape.

Linux has three system calls that skip that round trip: copy_file_range(2), sendfile(2), and splice(2). They look similar, but they solve different problems, and each has sharp edges that are easy to miss.

This is a practical tour: what each call actually guarantees, complete working code, how to fall back safely, and how to prove the copies are gone.

What the classic loop really costs

The read()/write() loop is not stupid. It is general: it works on sockets, pipes, character devices, and files, and it lets you inspect or transform the data. But for a plain file-to-file copy it does this:

  1. read() copies data from the page cache into your userspace buffer.
  2. write() copies it from your buffer into the destination's page cache.
  3. Writeback eventually sends it to storage.

Step 3 is unavoidable. Steps 1 and 2 are not. They also cost syscalls: two per buffer, plus scheduling and fault overhead.

The zero-copy calls push the copy down into the kernel, where it can move page references instead of bytes, or ask the filesystem to do something smarter.

Three calls, three shapes

Call Typical direction Key constraint Since
copy_file_range regular file → regular file both must be regular files; flags must be 0 Linux 4.5
sendfile regular file → socket (or file) input must support mmap-like operations Linux 2.2
splice anything ↔ pipe one descriptor must be a pipe Linux 2.6.17

The short version:

  • Copying a file to another file? Use copy_file_range.
  • Serving a file over a socket? Use sendfile.
  • Moving bytes between a socket and a file, or inserting a pipe into a pipeline? Use splice.
  • Need to inspect or modify the bytes? None of these help. Use read/write.

copy_file_range: the file-to-file default 

#define _GNU_SOURCE
#define _FILE_OFFSET_BITS 64
#include 

ssize_t copy_file_range(int fd_in, off_t *off_in,
                        int fd_out, off_t *off_out,
                        size_t size, unsigned int flags);

The contract, from copy_file_range(2):

  • If off_in is NULL, reading starts at the file offset and the offset advances. If it is non-NULL, the file offset is untouched and *off_in advances instead. The same applies to off_out.
  • The call returns the number of bytes copied, which may be less than requested. A return of 0 means the input offset is at or past EOF.
  • flags is reserved and must be 0.
  • fd_in and fd_out may refer to the same file, as long as the ranges do not overlap.
  • Both descriptors must refer to regular files (EINVAL otherwise), and fd_out must not have O_APPEND set.

The interesting part is what the man page calls "copy acceleration": the filesystem may implement the copy with reflinks (shared copy-on-write extents) or, on NFS, a server-side copy. You do not have to ask for it; the filesystem decides.

A complete, careful implementation

Short reads are normal, so the copy must loop. Cross-filesystem copies fail with EXDEV unless both filesystems are the same type and support it (since Linux 5.19), so a fallback is mandatory in portable code.

#define _GNU_SOURCE
#define _FILE_OFFSET_BITS 64
#include 
#include 
#include 
#include 
#include 
#include 
#include 
#include 

static int copy_rw(int in, int out)
{
    char buf[128 * 1024];

    for (;;) {
        ssize_t n = read(in, buf, sizeof buf);

        if (n == 0)
            return 0;
        if (n < 0) {
            if (errno == EINTR)
                continue;
            return -1;
        }

        char *p = buf;
        while (n > 0) {
            ssize_t w = write(out, p, (size_t)n);
            if (w < 0) {
                if (errno == EINTR)
                    continue;
                return -1;
            }
            p += w;
            n -= w;
        }
    }
}

static int copy_file(int in, int out, off_t size)
{
    off_t off_in = 0, off_out = 0;

    /* First choice: in-kernel file-to-file copy. */
    for (;;) {
        ssize_t n = copy_file_range(in, &off_in, out, &off_out, 1 << 20, 0);

        if (n > 0)
            continue;
        if (n == 0)
            return 0;
        if (errno == EINTR)
            continue;
        if (errno != EXDEV && errno != EINVAL &&
            errno != EOPNOTSUPP && errno != ENOSYS)
            return -1;
        break;  /* unsupported here; fall through */
    }

    /*
     * Resume exactly where copy_file_range stopped. Without these
     * lseeks a partially completed copy would be duplicated.
     */
    if (lseek(in, off_in, SEEK_SET) < 0)
        return -1;
    if (lseek(out, off_out, SEEK_SET) < 0)
        return -1;

    /* Second choice: sendfile to a regular file (Linux 2.6.33+). */
    while (off_in < size) {
        size_t chunk = (size_t)(size - off_in);
        if (chunk > 0x7ffff000)   /* sendfile's per-call limit */
            chunk = 0x7ffff000;

        ssize_t n = sendfile(out, in, &off_in, chunk);

        if (n > 0)
            continue;
        if (n == 0)
            return 0;
        if (errno == EINTR)
            continue;
        break;  /* sendfile refused too */
    }

    /* Last resort: the portable loop. */
    off_out = lseek(out, 0, SEEK_CUR);
    if (off_out < 0 || lseek(in, off_in, SEEK_SET) < 0)
        return -1;

    return copy_rw(in, out);
}

int main(int argc, char **argv)
{
    if (argc != 3) {
        fprintf(stderr, "usage: %s SRC DST\n", argv[0]);
        return 2;
    }

    int in = open(argv[1], O_RDONLY);
    if (in < 0) {
        perror("open src");
        return 1;
    }

    struct stat st;
    if (fstat(in, &st) < 0) {
        perror("fstat");
        return 1;
    }
    if (!S_ISREG(st.st_mode)) {
        fprintf(stderr, "%s: not a regular file\n", argv[1]);
        return 1;
    }

    int out = open(argv[2], O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, 0644);
    if (out < 0) {
        perror("open dst");
        return 1;
    }

    if (copy_file(in, out, st.st_size) < 0) {
        perror("copy");
        return 1;
    }

    /* copy_file_range copies bytes, not metadata. Do it yourself. */
    if (fchmod(out, st.st_mode & 07777) < 0)
        perror("fchmod");

    struct timespec ts[2] = { st.st_atim, st.st_mtim };
    if (futimens(out, ts) < 0)
        perror("futimens");

    close(out);
    close(in);
    return 0;
}

Build and run it:

cc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o zcopy zcopy.c
truncate -s 2G big.bin
./zcopy big.bin copy.bin

Two details in that code are worth staring at:

  • The fallback resumes at off_in/off_out. A partial copy_file_range followed by a naive copy_rw would append the whole file again.
  • sendfile is capped at 0x7ffff000 bytes per call on both 32-bit and 64-bit systems. That is 2,147,479,552 bytes, just under 2 GiB. Loop.

The sparse-file trap

copy_file_range(2) warns that holes in a sparse file may be expanded. In other words, a file that occupies 100 MB on disk but reports 10 GB of logical size can become a real 10 GB file after the copy. If sparseness matters, walk the file with lseek(SEEK_DATA) and lseek(SEEK_HOLE) and copy only the data segments, reproducing the holes with lseek and ftruncate on the destination.

sendfile: file to socket without the bounce 

#include 

ssize_t sendfile(int out_fd, int in_fd, off_t *offset, size_t count);

Note the argument order: output first. That surprises almost everyone once.

Facts that matter:

  • in_fd must support mmap-like operations, so it cannot be a socket. Since Linux 5.12, if out_fd is a pipe, sendfile simply becomes splice internally.
  • Before Linux 2.6.33, out_fd had to be a socket. Since then it can be any file, which is why sendfile appears in the fallback above.
  • The call transfers at most 0x7ffff000 bytes and may return a short count. Retry until done.
  • If offset is non-NULL, *offset is updated and the input file offset is left alone.

A minimal file server core:

{
    int fd = open(path, O_RDONLY);
    if (fd < 0)
        return -1;

    struct stat st;
    if (fstat(fd, &st) < 0) {
        close(fd);
        return -1;
    }

    char hdr[256];
    int hlen = snprintf(hdr, sizeof hdr,

Stop Bouncing Bytes Through User Space: Practical Zero-Copy File I/O on Linux

Every file copy you have ever written probably looks like this:

while ((n = read(in, buf, sizeof buf)) > 0)
    write(out, buf, n);

It is correct, portable, and quietly wasteful. For every byte, the kernel copies it from the page cache into your buffer, then from your buffer back into the page cache. On a 10 GB copy that is 20 GB of memory traffic that exists only to satisfy an API shape.

Linux has three system calls that skip that round trip: copy_file_range(2), sendfile(2), and splice(2). They look similar, but they solve different problems, and each has sharp edges that are easy to miss.

This is a practical tour: what each call actually guarantees, complete working code, how to fall back safely, and how to prove the copies are gone.

What the classic loop really costs

The read()/write() loop is not stupid. It is general: it works on sockets, pipes, character devices, and files, and it lets you inspect or transform the data. But for a plain file-to-file copy it does this:

  1. read() copies data from the page cache into your userspace buffer.
  2. write() copies it from your buffer into the destination's page cache.
  3. Writeback eventually sends it to storage.

Step 3 is unavoidable. Steps 1 and 2 are not. They also cost syscalls: two per buffer, plus scheduling and fault overhead.

The zero-copy calls push the copy down into the kernel, where it can move page references instead of bytes, or ask the filesystem to do something smarter.

Three calls, three shapes

Call Typical direction Key constraint Since
copy_file_range regular file → regular file both must be regular files; flags must be 0 Linux 4.5
sendfile regular file → socket (or file) input must support mmap-like operations Linux 2.2
splice anything ↔ pipe one descriptor must be a pipe Linux 2.6.17

The short version:

  • Copying a file to another file? Use copy_file_range.
  • Serving a file over a socket? Use sendfile.
  • Moving bytes between a socket and a file, or inserting a pipe into a pipeline? Use splice.
  • Need to inspect or modify the bytes? None of these help. Use read/write.

copy_file_range: the file-to-file default 

#define _GNU_SOURCE
#define _FILE_OFFSET_BITS 64
#include

                        int fd_out, off_t *off_out,
                        size_t size, unsigned int flags);

The contract, from copy_file_range(2):

  • If off_in is NULL, reading starts at the file offset and the offset advances. If it is non-NULL, the file offset is untouched and *off_in advances instead. The same applies to off_out.
  • The call returns the number of bytes copied, which may be less than requested. A return of 0 means the input offset is at or past EOF.
  • flags is reserved and must be 0.
  • fd_in and fd_out may refer to the same file, as long as the ranges do not overlap.
  • Both descriptors must refer to regular files (EINVAL otherwise), and fd_out must not have O_APPEND set.

The interesting part is what the man page calls "copy acceleration": the filesystem may implement the copy with reflinks (shared copy-on-write extents) or, on NFS, a server-side copy. You do not have to ask for it; the filesystem decides.

        if (n < 0) {

                continue;
            return -1;
        }

            if (w < 0) {

                    continue;
                return -1;
            }

            n -= w;
        }

    for (;;) {
        ssize_t n = copy_file_range(in, &off_in, out, &off_out, 1 << 20, 0);

        if (n > 0)
            continue;
        if (n == 0)
            return 0;
        if (errno == EINTR)
            continue;
        if (errno != EXDEV && errno != EINVAL &&
            errno != EOPNOTSUPP && errno != ENOSYS)
            return -1;
        break;  /* unsupported here; fall through */
    }

    /*

     * lseeks a partially completed copy would be duplicated.
     */
    if (lseek(in, off_in, SEEK_SET) < 0)
        return -1;
    if (lseek(out, off_out, SEEK_SET) < 0)
        return -1;

    while (off_in < size) {
        size_t chunk = (size_t)(size - off_in);
        if (chunk > 0x7ffff000)   /* sendfile's per-call limit */
            chunk = 0x7ffff000;

        ssize_t n = sendfile(out, in, &off_in, chunk);

        if (n > 0)
            continue;
        if (n == 0)
            return 0;
        if (errno == EINTR)
            continue;
        break;  /* sendfile refused too */
    }

    /* Last resort: the portable loop. */
    off_out = lseek(out, 0, SEEK_CUR);
    if (off_out < 0 || lseek(in, off_in, SEEK_SET) < 0)
        return -1;

    return copy_rw(in, out);
}

{
    if (argc != 3) {
        fprintf(stderr, "usage: %s SRC DST\n", argv[0]);
        return 2;
    }

    int in = open(argv[1], O_RDONLY);
    if (in < 0) {
        perror("open src");
        return 1;
    }

    struct stat st;
    if (fstat(in, &st) < 0) {
        perror("fstat");
        return 1;
    }
    if (!S_ISREG(st.st_mode)) {
        fprintf(stderr, "%s: not a regular file\n", argv[1]);
        return 1;
    }

    int out = open(argv[2], O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, 0644);
    if (out < 0) {
        perror("open dst");
        return 1;
    }

    if (copy_file(in, out, st.st_size) < 0) {
        perror("copy");
        return 1;
    }

    /* copy_file_range copies bytes, not metadata. Do it yourself. */
    if (fchmod(out, st.st_mode & 07777) < 0)
        perror("fchmod");

    struct timespec ts[2] = { st.st_atim, st.st_mtim };
    if (futimens(out, ts) < 0)

    close(out);
    close(in);
    return 0;
}

title: On-call handoff notes that people actually read
summary:
We used to write long handoff documents that nobody read. Now we write three lines and people actually use them.

The template:

  1. What's on fire (or nothing)
  2. What I changed that you should know about
  3. What I'm worried about

That's it. Three lines, posted in the on-call channel at handoff.

The surprising part: the third line is the most valuable. "I'm worried about the cron job that runs at 3am" has saved us several times.

We also added a rule: if you had a quiet week, say so explicitly. Silence is ambiguous; "nothing happened" is information.

Side quest: reading SQLite internals. WAL mode is a great case study in making a simple thing predictable.
